title: Handling disagreement
question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate. What was the disagreement, how did you handle it, and what happened?
followUps: What did you learn about your own approach?
What would you do differently now?

title: A setback
question: Tell me about a time something important did not go as planned. What did you do next?
followUps: What part was within your control?
How did you prevent the same issue later?

title: Leading without a title
question: Describe a time you helped a group make progress when nobody had clearly taken the lead.
followUps: How did you bring others along?
What resistance did you encounter?

title: A tight deadline
question: Tell me about a time you had several tasks competing for a tight deadline. How did you prioritize?
followUps: What did you choose not to do?
How did you keep others informed?

title: Receiving feedback
question: Describe useful critical feedback you received. How did you respond, and what changed afterward?
followUps: Was any part hard to hear?
What evidence shows you changed?

title: Taking initiative
question: Tell me about a problem you noticed and addressed before someone asked you to.
followUps: How did you decide it was worth addressing?
What was the measurable result?

title: Working with uncertainty
question: Describe a project where the requirements were unclear. How did you make progress without making risky assumptions?
followUps: What did you clarify first?
How did you validate your interpretation?

title: Strong collaboration
question: Tell me about a time a team achieved a good result because people with different strengths worked well together.
followUps: What did you personally contribute?
How did the team handle different working styles?

title: Owning a mistake
question: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected someone else or a project. How did you address it?
followUps: How quickly did you raise it?
What safeguard did you add?

title: Persuading with evidence
question: Describe a time you changed someone's mind or helped a group choose a direction. What evidence did you use?
followUps: What did the other person care about?
What would you have done if they still disagreed?

title: A result you are proud of
question: Which accomplishment are you proudest of, and what was your specific contribution to it?
followUps: What was difficult about it?
How did you measure success?

title: Changing priorities
question: Tell me about a time priorities changed suddenly. How did you adjust while keeping important work on track?
followUps: What did you pause or renegotiate?
Who needed to know about the change?

title: Estimate campus coffee demand
question: Estimate how many cups of coffee are bought on your campus on a typical weekday. Talk through your assumptions and calculation.
focus: Defining scope, assumptions, and a sanity check
followUps: Which assumption affects your answer most?
How would you validate your estimate quickly?

title: Estimate buses in a city
question: Estimate how many city buses are needed to serve a mid-sized Indian city during peak hours.
focus: Segmenting demand, capacity, and peak utilization
followUps: How would the answer change on a weekend?
What data would you request first?

title: Estimate pizzas for an event
question: A college is hosting a 500-person evening event. Estimate how many pizzas to order and explain how you would reduce waste.
focus: Demand segments, serving sizes, and uncertainty
followUps: What if attendance is uncertain by 20%?
What would you do with leftovers?

title: Estimate daily phone charging
question: Estimate the electricity used to charge smartphones in a college hostel in one day.
focus: Units, population, usage assumptions, and magnitude check
followUps: Which device assumption matters most?
How could you cross-check the result?

title: Estimate a busy junction
question: Estimate how many vehicles pass through a busy four-way junction in one hour.
focus: Traffic-light cycles, lanes, and vehicle mix
followUps: How would you account for motorcycles?
What observation would improve the estimate?

title: Estimate water use
question: Estimate the daily water demand for a 1,000-student college campus.
focus: Breaking demand into people, uses, and non-student needs
followUps: How would holidays affect it?
Where is the biggest uncertainty?

title: Estimate lift capacity
question: A 12-floor office has 600 employees. Estimate how many lifts it needs to keep morning waits reasonable.
focus: Arrival patterns, lift capacity, and wait-time goals
followUps: Which assumption would you test first?
What low-cost alternative could reduce demand?

title: Estimate daily searches
question: Estimate the number of search queries made by people in a city of one million in a day.
focus: Population segments and queries per person
followUps: How would you avoid false precision?
What independent check could you use?

title: A service outage
question: A feature you own stops working for many users just before a major deadline. What do you do in the first 30 minutes?
focus: Triage, user impact, communication, and recovery
followUps: What would make you roll back?
How would you communicate uncertainty?

title: An unclear assignment
question: Your manager asks for an analysis but gives no definition of success and is unavailable for two days. How do you proceed?
focus: Clarifying what you can, making assumptions visible, and limiting rework
followUps: What would you deliver first?
How would you document assumptions?

title: A struggling teammate
question: A teammate is missing commitments and the team's deadline is at risk. What would you do?
focus: Empathy, direct communication, and protecting delivery
followUps: What if the pattern continues?
How do you avoid taking over their work?

title: Disagreeing with a manager
question: Your manager chooses an approach you believe will fail. How would you raise your concern?
focus: Evidence, respect, and commitment after a decision
followUps: What if the decision stays the same?
What evidence would change your view?

title: Reducing project scope
question: A project is behind schedule and cannot meet every requirement. How would you decide what to cut?
focus: User value, risk, dependencies, and transparent trade-offs
followUps: What would you preserve at all costs?
How would you explain the cut to stakeholders?

title: Questionable data
question: Your analysis suggests a surprising result, but one dataset looks unreliable. How would you present your findings?
followUps: What checks would you run?
What can you responsibly conclude now?

title: Two urgent requests
question: Two senior colleagues give you urgent tasks with the same deadline. How do you handle the conflict?
followUps: What if both insist theirs comes first?
How do you keep both informed?

title: A tool you have never used
question: You are assigned a task using a tool you have never used, and the deadline is close. What is your plan?
focus: Learning quickly, seeking help, and managing risk
followUps: How do you decide what to learn first?
When would you ask for a different approach?

title: An upset user
question: A user is upset because a change your team made disrupted their work. How would you respond?
followUps: What if you cannot fix it immediately?
How do you prevent a repeat?

title: Automating a manual process
question: A team spends hours each week on repetitive manual work. How would you decide whether to automate it?
focus: Frequency, error cost, maintenance, and return on effort
followUps: When would automation be a bad idea?
How would you measure the result?

title: Your introduction
question: Tell me about yourself in about 90 seconds, focusing on what is relevant to the role you want.
focus: A clear through-line, relevant evidence, and a natural ending
followUps: Which experience best shows your strengths?
Why are you interested in this kind of work?

title: Why this role?
question: Why are you interested in this role, and what would you hope to contribute in your first year?
followUps: What have you learned about the work?
Which skill would you need to build first?

title: A strength with evidence
question: What is one strength you would bring to a team? Give a concrete example that shows it.
followUps: When has this strength been less useful?
How have others noticed it?

title: A growth area
question: What is a skill or habit you are actively trying to improve, and what are you doing about it?
followUps: How will you know you are improving?
What feedback have you received about it?

title: What motivates you?
question: What kind of work gives you energy, and how have you acted on that in a project or course?
focus: Authentic motivation grounded in an example
followUps: What work drains your energy?
How do you stay effective when a task is less interesting?

title: Why should we hire you?
question: Why should we choose you for this opportunity? Make a focused case using evidence, not just adjectives.
focus: Role fit, proof, and a concise close
followUps: What would you need support with?
What differentiates your approach?

title: A value you act on
question: What value matters to you at work, and tell me about a time it influenced a decision you made.
focus: Consistency between stated value and action
followUps: Was there a trade-off?
Would you make the same choice now?

title: Your next few years
question: What would you like to learn or be trusted with over the next few years?
followUps: What are you doing now to prepare?
How might your goals change?

title: Explain a project
question: Explain a project you worked on to someone outside your field. What problem did it solve and what did you do?
focus: Plain language, personal contribution, and outcome
followUps: What was the hardest decision?
What would you improve next?

title: A challenge you are addressing
question: What work-related challenge do you find difficult, and what practical steps are you taking to manage it?
followUps: When does it show up most?
What has helped so far?

title: Questions for the interviewer
question: At the end of an interview, what thoughtful questions would you ask about the team, expectations, or success in the role?
focus: Curiosity and questions that reveal useful information
followUps: Which answer would affect your decision most?
How would you ask about feedback and growth?

title: A gap in your experience
question: How would you respond if an interviewer points out that you have limited experience in one requirement of the role?
focus: Honesty, transferable evidence, and a learning plan
followUps: What evidence can you offer instead?
How would you close the gap?

title: Fair credit
question: A teammate presents a group result as if they did most of the work. How would you respond?
followUps: Would you address it privately first?
How would you protect the working relationship?

title: A risky shortcut
question: You notice a shortcut that could make a deadline but might create a serious quality issue. What would you do?
followUps: What facts would you gather first?
How could you preserve the deadline safely?

title: Confidential information
question: A colleague asks you to share information you are not sure they are allowed to see. How do you handle it?
followUps: Who could clarify access?
What if the request is urgent?

title: Reporting a quality issue
question: You find a significant error in work that has already been shared with a client. What do you do?
focus: Prompt disclosure, impact reduction, and accountability
followUps: What would you say first?
How would you prevent recurrence?

title: An unfair team decision
question: You believe a team decision treats one person unfairly, but raising it may be uncomfortable. How would you proceed?
focus: Specific observations, respectful challenge, and safe escalation
followUps: How would you distinguish facts from assumptions?
What if the first conversation changes nothing?

title: A misleading metric
question: Someone asks you to present a metric in a way that makes results look better than they are. What would you do?
followUps: How can you keep the presentation useful?
What if they insist?

title: When you do not know
question: An interviewer asks a technical question and you do not know the answer. Talk through what you would say and do.
focus: Composure, honest boundaries, and reasoning aloud
followUps: What related knowledge could you use?
How would you follow up afterward?

title: Recovering after an interruption
question: You are halfway through an answer when the interviewer interrupts and redirects you. How do you respond?
followUps: How do you make sure you answered the new question?
What if you still need to complete an important point?

title: Answer in 30 seconds
question: In 30 seconds, explain one reason you are ready for your first professional role.
followUps: What detail did you leave out deliberately?
How would you expand it if asked?

title: Challenge your own idea
question: Present a recommendation you believe in, then explain the strongest argument against it and how you would test which view is right.
followUps: What result would change your mind?
What is the downside of waiting for more data?

title: A skeptical follow-up
question: You say you are a strong problem solver. An interviewer asks, ‘What evidence do you have?’ Give a specific, concise example.
followUps: What was your individual contribution?
What was the result?

title: Reframing a difficult question
question: An interviewer asks about a result that fell short of your goal. Answer honestly while showing what you learned and changed.
followUps: What responsibility was yours?
What changed in your next attempt?
